name: Beaucaire
lede: Beaucaire is a muted greenish blue recorded in Maerz and Paul's 1930 color dictionary, close enough to the library's Dirty Blue and Cerulean that only a few measured units separate them.

sections.title: A 1925 entry, no story behind it
sections.body:
Maerz and Paul's *A Dictionary of Color* (1930) places Beaucaire on plate 35, position L4, and dates its first recorded use to 1925 [1]. The dictionary gives no account of where the name comes from, so its origin is undocumented here [1]. The ISCC-NBS lists of 1955 do not carry the name separately; the National Bureau of Standards circular only cites Maerz and Paul's entry [1].

The library's own measurements put this swatch closest to [[chessylite-blue|Dirty Blue]], 3.2 units off, a slightly greyer, darker blue, and within a few units of [[cerulean|Cerulean]], which is brighter and leans more toward pure blue [2]. By the color-matching math it also sits near the ISCC-NBS block for *vivid greenish blue*, about five and a half units off, though no book files Beaucaire there directly [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Our archive finds a color match to this swatch in 69 of 23,781 paintings, 0.29 percent, as photographed; the stricter within-painting lens finds it in 30 [3]. That makes it rarer than 57 percent of the named colors we track [3]. Claude Monet is its most devoted painter here, carrying it in 4 of the 50 [[painter:claude-monet|Monet]] paintings in the archive, 6.7 times the rate expected from the museums his works come from [3].

Usage peaks in the 1900s, with 7 of 1,674 paintings from that decade carrying it, three times the expected rate, and inside a painting it most often sits as an accent rather than a dominant field (43 percent of its 30 within-painting matches) [3]. The earliest match is Marco Zoppo's panel of 1467, nearly five centuries before the name's 1925 record, which shows only that a similar-looking hue existed in paint long before the word did, not that the pigment or dye did, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [3]. France is the most over-represented country, at 2.4 times its expected share [3]. These are photographs of varnished paintings, read as screen colors [3].
